analysis.one_liner: Requires 100% renewable electricity by 2035 and steep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions through 2050.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in committee for the entire Congress and never received a vote, despite 24 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force electric utilities to sell electricity made entirely from renewable sources by 2035, require utilities and gas suppliers to hit rising energy-saving targets, and direct the EPA to set pollution limits cutting U.S. greenhouse gas emissions to at least 40% below 1990 levels by 2035 and 80% below by 2050. It never got a hearing or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing climate damages — floods, wildfires, extreme heat, higher food and insurance costs — plus the renewable energy industry, which gains a guaranteed market as utilities must buy renewable power, and consumers whose utility efficiency programs lower bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and the renewable energy industry

how_it_helps.text: Mandates that 100% of electricity sold in the U.S. come from renewable sources by 2035, accelerating the shift off fossil-fuel power plants.
Requires retail electric and gas suppliers to deliver rising annual energy-efficiency savings to customers, which lowers household energy bills.
Directs EPA to set binding emission-reduction targets through 2050, reviewed every five years, to keep U.S. climate pledges on track.
Lets suppliers meet efficiency targets through a market-based trading system, lowering compliance costs.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil-fuel power generators and coal, oil, and gas interests lose guaranteed sales as utilities shift to renewables; utilities bear compliance costs, some of which could show up in electricity rates during the transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel power generators and utilities

drawbacks.text: Reaching 100% renewable electricity by 2035 is an aggressive timeline; building the needed transmission, storage, and generation could raise electricity prices in some regions and strain the grid.
The bill relies on regulation without funding for workers or communities displaced from fossil-fuel jobs, unlike some competing climate proposals.
Efficiency and renewable mandates fall on utilities, and compliance costs can be passed to ratepayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The climate damages the bill aims to prevent — sea-level rise, wildfires, extreme weather — vastly exceed the compliance costs in mainstream economic analysis, but the aggressive 2035 timeline and lack of transition support for fossil-fuel workers and coal communities are real weaknesses an honest supporter would concede.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs committees on introduction, then to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change, where it sat with no hearings, markups, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in January 2019 by Rep. Ted Lieu with 24 Democratic cosponsors.
Referred to House Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs committees; later referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change.
No further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fuel generators and utilities that would have faced binding renewable and efficiency mandates benefit from the bill's inaction, as do members opposed to climate mandates who avoided a recorded vote.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 24 cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda in the 116th Congress and did not bring climate mandate legislation to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-held Senate and White House made passage implausible regardless.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas power generators
industries.note: The 100% renewable mandate and EPA emission targets would phase out fossil-fueled electricity sales; the industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the public's interest in lower climate damages and cleaner air.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and utility-scale solar/wind developers
industries.note: A binding national renewable standard guarantees a growing market for renewable generation through 2035.
Utilities bear the cost of compliance — buying renewable power and funding efficiency programs — though some costs can be recovered through rates.
Mandated annual efficiency savings create demand for efficiency upgrades and services.
